speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also thank all Members who have expressed their desire to voice supporting speeches.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, I would like to express my gratitude to the Minister for Home Affairs who was very supportive of the idea of this Motion when Mr Murali Pillai and I broached the idea of it and also for agreeing to speak on it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) has come a long way since its beginnings in 1820.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Francis James Bernard led Singapore's first Police force with just 12 officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SPF has done a lot for Singapore over the last 200 years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the early colonial times, Singapore faced many challenges in law and order, such as gambling, prostitution, opium abuse and secret society activities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There were conflicts and unrest between the different communities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Faction fighting, robberies, murders and the use of firearms were so rampant in the 1920s that some nicknamed Singapore the "Chicago of the East".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After World War Two, there was social disorder and conflict between people of different backgrounds and ideologies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unions and schools were infiltrated by communists and their supporters who instigated riots and public unrest in the Chinese middle schools.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Discontent and distrust brewed between different races, resulting in racially-charged riots.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The capabilities of the Police grew to meet these new challenges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Part-time National Service was operationalised in SPF in 1967 to augment manpower resources.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two years later, the Government expanded the recruitment of Police officers and reorganised the Police Academy in 1969 to equip recruits with the skills for effective policing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the 1980s, SPF explored new ways to directly engage residents in fighting crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides the Neighbourhood Watch Scheme, we also formed the National Crime Prevention Council.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Neighbourhood Police Posts and Neighbourhood Police Centres were set up to bring policing to the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This transformed the image of the Police officer, not just as a person enforcing the law, but to also being a trusted member of the community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the last two decades, SPF has enhanced its capabilities to meet new and complex challenges beyond neighbourhood crime, such as terrorism, cybercrime, commercial crime and scams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All these efforts brought about the low crime rates that we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This safety and security underpinned Singapore's remarkable growth and progress.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the years, SPF has successfully upheld safety and security at several major events hosted by Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are complex security operations that require close coordination across different SPF teams covering various aspects of security, including patrols, monitoring the ground and being prepared to stop any threats that may arise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, SPF has to ensure that daily operational needs were not compromised even as it dedicated resources to the smooth running of these events.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the security operations for our National Day Parades require extensive planning and seamless execution by many SPF ground units.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Members would also recall the Trump-Kim Summit which Singapore hosted in June 2018.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The short lead time and volatility of plans made planning for the security operations extremely challenging.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SPF made meticulous and detailed plans for the security operations in coordination with Home Team agencies and other public agencies, with many – I should emphasise "many" – different security contingency plans worked out.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SPF has also effectively managed complex security operations at many other events that bring together international guests to Singapore, such as the Shangri-La Dialogues, Formula One races and Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation or APEC meetings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For each of these events, SPF assesses the security risks, crafts detailed security plans and executes these plans effectively in close coordination with other agencies, if required.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SPF's tireless efforts have contributed to the successful hosting of these events, boosting the Republic of Singapore's reputation globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SPF has also contributed significantly to combatting transnational crime through international policing work in cooperation with its foreign counterparts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SPF has mounted many successful operations in collaboration with its foreign counterparts over the years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, in 2020, officers from the Commercial Affairs Department collaborated with the Hong Kong Police Force to arrest five core members of a transnational online credit card fraud syndicate operating in Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2020, the Commercial Affairs Department also worked with the Royal Malaysia Police to conduct a joint police operation against a transnational Internet scam syndicated in Kuala Lumpur.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am also told that our SPF has strong ties with Indonesia and its police force.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2008, then-Commissioner of Police Khoo Boon Hui was elected as President of INTERPOL by an overwhelming majority vote.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In SPF's early history, it would have been unthinkable for Singapore's Police force to be able to contribute anything substantial to international policing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two centuries on, SPF is one of the leading police forces in the world, playing a significant role in international crime-fighting efforts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are proud of SPF and its many achievements over the last 200 years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, we are privileged to have in the House, 69 visitors representing the SPF family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They include Singapore's Commissioner of Police, in-service officers, full-time National Servicemen, Operationally Ready National Servicemen, Volunteer Special Constabulary officers, civilian officers, retired Police officers and two family members of a Police officer who was killed in the line of duty.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Your presence here today, allows us to honour, in a special way, the whole of the Singapore Police Force and the families of our officers, past and present.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On a more personal note, I would like to share that I have seen the dedication and courage of our Police officers at close range.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the course of my membership in the Government Parliamentary Committee or GPC for Home Affairs and Law, I have visited the Police on the ground, spoken with many officers and witnessed operational exercises, including anti-terror exercises.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) has, over two centuries since the founding of modern Singapore, made Singapore one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This security which allows us all to walk safe at night, to work without fear in the day, this peace of mind, is a public good without price.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We honour SPF officers, past and present, for their courage and unwavering sense of duty; we remember those who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the past and those who walk the streets each day, know that this sacrifice may be demanded of them in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I would like to focus on the contributions of our retired SPF officers as well as the sacrifice of officers who gave up their lives in the course of their duties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A good number of them joined service in the 1960s and the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In those days, we had serious issues in enforcing law and order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, we had to contend with the menace of secret societies, a point that hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: SPF needed stout-hearted people to deal with these problems.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thankfully, it had a good number of such officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Detective Station Inspector Anthony Low joined SPF in 1962.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1974, Mr Low, then a detective sergeant, was called to attend to a case of an armed robbery in progress at a finance company.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He forced the manager of the company to draw money from a bank and bring it back to her office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The manager tipped off her colleague before leaving for the bank.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Low laid an ambush in the office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The robber entered the office, but somehow sensed danger and rushed out.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is useful for me to pause here and explain the significance of this to hon Members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I am relating is not a movie scene.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a case of an officer chasing a robber known to be armed with a gun.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst climbing up the staircase of a building looking for the robber, the robber in turn ambushed Mr Low.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He struck Mr Low on his head with the butt of his revolver repeatedly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The robber then relieved Mr Low of his service gun and tucked it into his waist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He then said the chilling words, "Why do you want to risk your life looking for me?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today is my day or yours." He then asked Mr Low to walk down the stairs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Low seized an opportunity to grab his service gun from the robber's waist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The robber then took a step backward to fire at him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: DSI Low went on to have an illustrious career in SPF and retired after 40 years of service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Lim Siong, who is also in this House, served in Security Branch, now known as the Police Security Command, before retiring as a Station Inspector in 1993.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For a good number of years, he was one of the Security Officers in the team assigned to protect Mr Lee Kuan Yew, our founding Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These security officers, past and present, are a special breed of people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Their training, their muscle memory is to put themselves in harm's way to protect our nation's leaders, if necessary, with their lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Lim Siong joined SPF in 1968 when Police officers still wore khaki shorts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apparently, the idea was to keep them cool in the day.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1969, when the then Constable Lim Siong was on duty, he received information that there was a suspicious person lurking around the railway tracks beside the old Chartered Bank along Upper Bukit Timah Road.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With his baton, he managed to disarm and handcuff the person by himself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He then recovered the bomb, which was in a Milo tin, and the communist flag from the scene.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, these items can be seen at ISD's Heritage Centre.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Lim Siong's quick thinking and fearlessness saved lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Just two weeks later, however, sadly, a bomb did explode at Upper Changi Road, Seven Mile, killing a lady.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members would agree that there has been a sea change in the crime and security situation in Singapore since the 1960s and 1970s.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is our good fortune that SPF could count on its brave and dedicated officers who turned the tide against crime and disorder.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is no doubt in my mind that SPF today stands on the shoulders of these giants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To them, I would like, on behalf of a grateful nation, to express a debt of enduring thanks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now wish to pay tribute to our Police officers killed in the line of duty and their families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I would imagine more officers would have perished in SPF's 200-year history.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am indebted to the Commissioner of Police for providing me with a list of the officers who have been killed in the line of duty and I seek your permission to annex this list to my speech, please.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One of the officers in the list was the late Inspector Allan Lim Kim Sai.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He was a second generation Police officer, following the footsteps of his father who joined the Police force when we were still part of the Straits Settlement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The gangster even lobbed hand grenades which exploded, causing injuries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the time when Inspector Lim died, his only son, David Lim, was just nine months old.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The responsibility to take care of David fell fully on his mother.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Raised by his mother, he too, like his grandfather and his father before him, joined the Singapore Police Force in 1992.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: When he reported for duty, after nine months of Police training, in 1993 at Tanglin Police Division, he asked Mr Peter Lim, his head of department who was a colleague of the late Inspector Allan Lim and present in this House today, "Tell me, how did my father die?" Mdm Deputy Speaker, Mr David Lim is in this House today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He retired as a Superintendent of Police two years ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I extended an invitation to his mother, who is now 84, to attend Parliament.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Unfortunately, she is not fit enough to travel.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One other person's name that appears in the list of 125 officers is the late SI Boo Tiang Huat.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I was his colleague then and I was at the scene several minutes after he perished.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I spoke about the anguish his widow and three young children felt when I accompanied them to the location he passed away to pray for his soul later that day.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: SI Boo Tiang Huat's widow, Mdm Chew Tuan Jong, is present in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So is her son, Mr Boo Jia Liang.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I remembered Jia Liang as a seven-year-old boy with spiky hair.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: All three graduated from University; two of them, including Jia Liang, became teachers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Jia Liang shared with me that, knowing how hard his mother worked to raise him and his siblings, all three siblings decided that she should retire 10 years ago and just enjoy life whilst they take full care of her.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For the officers who died in the line of duty, their spouses, parents, children and siblings bore the brunt of the loss.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Widows of fallen officers like Mrs Lim and Mdm Chew would have to dig deep to raise their children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Children of the fallen officers like David and Jia Liang would forever wonder how life would have been for them if only their fathers had come home.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As a nation, we should never forget the ultimate sacrifices made by our fallen SPF officers in the line of duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But we should also not forget the extraordinary courage of the families of the these fallen officers too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They deserve not just our appreciation, but to be remembered and honoured too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the past five decades, since as a little boy, I have had the honour of seeing, witnessing, working in, serving in and partnering many in the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During the first 10 years of my life, my late cousin, who lived with me, served in SPF in Team Policing and in Criminal Investigations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I saw for myself, as a young boy, the dedication and service to the nation of our Police officers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Oftentimes, the work involves long shifts, sudden recalls and chasing criminals until they are apprehended.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: He rose through the ranks as a Constable to a senior Police officer before he retired from SPF.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Through him, I saw how every Police officer, regardless of rank, unit or type of work, plays an important role in ensuring the safety and security of our country.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During the second 10 years of my life, my encounter with SPF came in the form of my extra-curricular activity in school in the National Police Cadet Corp (NPCC) for four years from Secondary 1 to Secondary 4.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Little known, the NPCC under the auspices of SPF, commemorating their 62nd anniversary this year, has impacted many youths and young people like me.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Besides having the opportunity to fire a 0.22 Smith & Wesson Revolver, the NPCC imparted many useful experiences, knowledge and life skills to many young people and youths.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I was at their 62nd virtual anniversary celebrations on 7 May this year and want to congratulate the NPCC movement and everyone who has been and is part of this movement for leaving an indelible mark on many who have been through the NPCC journey in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During the third 10 years of my life, in my 20s, I spent six years of it with the SPF as a full-time Police officer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I cannot divulge more of the highly secretive, dangerous and risky training and operations which these units have been involved in, but you can watch subtle snippets of it in archived episodes of Crimewatch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I know many of my fellow officers put our lives at risk undergoing very intense, gruelling training in the operations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In fact, not just putting their lives at risk but also affecting lots of family life and time with family.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Two very impressionable ones were when I had to stand my wife up in the midst of a midnight movie, because I had a pager call for an activation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Another time, over a dinner date, I had to walk out in the middle of the dinner; both for important criminal operations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I think the efforts and contributions of our SPF cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In fact, in the course of my career in SPF, there were a few officers who left a very lasting impression on me; both whom I reported to and worked with: Mr Lim Soo Gee, then Commander, Special Operations Command, and Director Operations SPF then, Mr Leo Yip, as well as current Commissioner of Police, Hoong Wee Teck, whom we used to, in colloquial terms, "chiong sua" together, when he was then AD Major Crime of the Criminal Investigation Department.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Oftentimes, their work may go unnoticed but I can assure you these units are highly trained and provide SPF with specialised tactical support and the highest armed response, a plethora of operational capabilities, and operational readiness to stand ready for the unexpected and overcome any unplanned contingencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During my 30s, after leaving SPF, I was in active service as a NSman in the Police Training Command.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I met and interacted with many SPF NSmen during my annual recall for about a decade.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I want to, therefore, use this opportunity to thank and appreciate them and their families and employers, as they complement and support SPF especially during major national events, critical operations and deployments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: An often-forgotten group will be the VSC officers who are civilian volunteers, who also dedicate their personal time to serve and patrol alongside our SPF officers on the ground.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the last 10 years as a Member of Parliament, I have had the chance to also partner and work with the SPF line units to see to the safety and security of the constituency and our residents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To conclude, I wish to express my heartfelt thanks, appreciation, respect and honour to the many members of SPF, past and present, young and not so young, enlisting, entering or have retired or left us, NS or regular or VSC, Uniformed or Non-Uniformed, including the many families, wives, children, parents and loved ones of each of them for their dedicated service, working tirelessly, upholding the law, often putting their lives at risk and at stake to nation building and to keeping Singapore one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The work of SPF will continue, and if I may use my favourite quotation from George Orwell: "People sleep peaceably at night because rough men" – well, and women – "stand ready to do battle on their behalf." Happy SPF 200.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The three Members of the House who have filed the Motion and supported it, understand what Police work entails; being a former prosecutor and two former Police officers respectively.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Force and its officers have had to continually adapt and raise their game to be equal to these challenges.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is also not easy to manage the ever-increasing expectations of the public who, in this digital age, expect quick turnaround times and instant answers from investigators through WhatsApp.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My Party colleague, Mr Dennis Tan, will speak more about the work of SPF in the community.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, we should also be mindful that there are other police forces working in, arguably, even tougher conditions, perhaps, because the police are unarmed as in the UK or because the public has the right to carry firearms, as in the US.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my speech today, I shall resist the temptation to reminisce about my late father's involvement in the Operation in 1965, just described by Member of Parliament, Mr Murali, where Inspector Allan Lim was fatally shot, nor shall I dwell on my experiences as a law enforcement officer in the 1990s.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, several Members of this House are former officers with longer and deeper insights.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, that we should not forget the co-equal contributions made by other agencies and, second, that effective policing is not just about safety and security alone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, I acknowledge that it is quite natural to focus on the Police as the pre-eminent law enforcement agency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, keeping Singapore safe is also done every day by many other agencies as well as private sector organisations, whom I feel are often not acknowledged enough.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These agencies should also occupy the public mind share as co-equal contributors to the state of Singapore security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It gives comfort to citizens and makes it attractive to foreigners to come here to live and work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Despite this strength, I wish to emphasise that effective policing should not be measured only by this metric of law and order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now turn to the second point of my speech.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Imagine, hypothetically, if one were to be confronted with the statistic, that every arrest by law enforcement officers resulted in a conviction in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, a 100% success rate may seem truly impressive, but on further reflection, a reasonable person would want to drill further down into the reasons for this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Questions such as the following would be asked: how did the law enforcement officers get it right every single time?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Were they so careful to only arrest suspects when the evidence was overwhelming?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And if trials were conducted, how did the judges assess the evidence?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If a society were to be absolutely safe, one could go overboard and lock up as many people as possible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is not as ridiculous as it sounds, as it is an accepted dilemma faced by governments and law enforcement all over the world.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Students of Criminal Justice learn very early about Herbert Packer's two models of criminal justice developed in the 1960s: the crime control model and the due process model.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A crime control model focuses on efficiency and crime suppression, seeing crime control as more important than individual freedom.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, a due process model focuses on having a just and fair criminal justice system for all and upholding constitutional rights.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Every criminal justice system worth its salt will have to find its balance between the two models.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While it seems to me that many Singaporeans would prioritise crime control, fair-minded Singaporeans would also want a system where law enforcement agencies must produce evidence of a high standard before anyone is convicted and punished.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I would urge the Government to look into finding the resources to enable law enforcement to perform their roles more effectively.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For today, I will take just two aspects: recording of statements and supporting crime victims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the debate on the Justice Motion last November, my party colleagues and I pointed to certain aspects of the justice system where more could be done to ensure its fairness, accessibility and independence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the main, the Government did not disagree with us, stating that we were "pushing an open door." To that end, it seems to me that some review of priorities should be considered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, on the way statements are recorded from suspects, we know that video-recording is a good safeguard to ensure that statements are not coerced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We heard from the Minister then that video-recording was the gold standard but resources were a constraint.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I suggested recording statements in other languages for suspects not fluent in English, I was told that it was not possible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But these are being done in other countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for our response towards crime victims, my assessment is that we lag behind other countries in our measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be fair, there have been some steps in this direction to recognise crime victims as stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe these measures are not used in the vast majority of Court cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had spoken about this last November and will not repeat further here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Suffice to say, victims are stakeholders and their cooperation can make or break a case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, we must not neglect the training of law enforcement officers in critical soft skills that will make them more effective.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have highlighted today that even as the Police has indeed been at the forefront of keeping Singapore safe, other agencies have as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Having more inclusive case processes would also be in order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I support the Motion, we should not think that we have arrived but strive for even higher standards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are also living at a time when the public's expectation of Police standard is increasing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, the video-recorded interview of suspects has been introduced a few years ago and many hope that it will be extensively used.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Today, I wish to spend a little time on the Police work in our neighbourhoods and community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Since I became the Member of Parliament for Hougang, I have had many opportunities to see our SPF officers doing their work in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also heard much from my residents of their own experience with our Police officers when they have had the need to contact them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Recently, one of my elderly residents passed away suddenly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Officers from the Hougang Neighbourhood Police Centre (NPC) and Ang Mo Kio Police Division had to attend onsite to do the necessary investigation before helping staff of a casket company to remove the body.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I had a great view of their professional efforts on display that evening as I witnessed the Police officers going about the grim but necessary work competently, meticulously and coolly even as it was not the most pleasant vocation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The officers, including a young NSF officer, handled the grieving relatives onsite professionally and calmly and yet, empathetically, patiently making sure that the next-of-kin knew what was going on and what the relatives had to do next.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Police officers in our NPC attend to many calls every day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am sure they deal with all types of crime reporting.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But they also deal with noisy or unruly behaviour at void decks, fights, families' or neighbours' disputes, suicides or unnatural deaths, fires in HDB flats or common spaces and many others.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In recent times, they also had to handle many scamming cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am often amazed by the range of cases for which people make Police reports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many reports probably involve issues which do not come under Police jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But one can just imagine the amount of time taken by our Police officers in NPCs, Police stations and Police posts, helping members of the public to patiently record their Police reports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A lot of such work can be mundane, dreary and thankless.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It may not be as exciting or headline grabbing as cyber crimes, fraud or other white-collar crimes, drugs and vice-related offences or even checking on KTVs or gambling dens but a large number of our Police officers have to do such unglamorous but necessary bread and butter community policing work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The work they do in a community is necessary and help to keep things in the right equilibrium and will help to make our homes, neighbourhoods and towns feel safer, more secure and peaceful.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Save for a few isolated incidents, by and large, we do not usually feel unsafe when we walk around any part of Singapore at any time of the day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many people, both locally and abroad, have pointed to Singapore having fewer violent crimes on our streets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is, of course, not something which we can ever take for granted and SPF must continue to work on this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We are also one of the few countries where many of our Police officers are NSF officers freshly enlisted from school at the cusp of adulthood.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The different challenges that our young NSF Police officers may have to face every day cannot be underestimated and can be daunting.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that our young NSF Police officers are given sufficient psychological support as they go about their work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In Committee of Supply debates for MHA in recent years, Members of Parliament have brought up the issue of manpower constraints in SPF.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More use of technology, while necessary, can never make up for the human touch, the need for a good relationship with the community as well as for more empathy when handling members of the public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Good relationships between Police officers and residents in the community will promote mutual trust, which is essential for effective policing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should also be mindful that – and I quote from an article from a US Department of Justice community relations services toolkit for policing entitled "The Importance of Police-Community Relationships and Resources for Further Reading" – "the community members' willingness to trust the police depends on whether they believe that police actions reflect community values and incorporate the principles of procedural justice and legitimacy".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Good relationships and trust will enhance officers' efforts on the ground when they engage residents and will also encourage provision of information important for solving of crimes or non-crime matters handled by the Police.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, I commend SPF for the good work which its officers do in its community policing efforts on an everyday basis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Police work is challenging, not simply because the job of keeping Singapore safe and secure never ends, but also because most of the work that our Police officers do daily goes unseen, often unknown and, hence, unrecognised.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, I would like to join my Parliamentary colleagues in honouring the tireless efforts made by our Police officers, particularly, the invisible work that is done to keep Singapore and Singaporeans safe every day and every night.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the name suggests, the primary role of an intelligence officer is to provide intelligence: critical information that can help solve a case or prevent a harm from happening.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But this is not as simple as it sounds.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Intelligence work can mean poring through large amounts of data, analysing heaps of spreadsheets and documents, and reviewing long hours of CCTV footages or it could mean going undercover for weeks or laying in ambush for days, sometimes to no avail.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As a former Police commander, I valued very much the hard work and contributions of our Police intelligence officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For obvious reasons, I cannot say more on what they do but their efforts are tremendous and often unknown to the public.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, today, in this House, I would like to extend my appreciation to all the dedicated men and women in our Police intelligence service who work quietly behind the scenes all these years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Next, I would like to highlight another vital but often unseen policing unit, the Police Coast Guard (PCG).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They patrol and protect Singapore's territorial waters, a job that is often confused with our more famous Navy counterparts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As an island state, threats from our territorial waters are plentiful and our PCG officers deal with a variety of challenges every day, and especially so in the darkness of night, ranging from piracy attacks to detecting and deterring illegal persons from swimming across the sea to enter or leave Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: No matter how choppy the waters are, we can always count on the Singapore Police Coast Guard to keep our waters safe.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Moving inland, I would like to commend the work of another important Police unit which has kept a low-profile presence since it was established in 1949, the Gurkha Contingent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The first batch of Gurkha officers arrived in Singapore in March 1949.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Known for their courage, loyalty and paramilitary prowess, they guard our vital installations and provide security coverage for major events held in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Gurkhas were first called to the frontlines in the 1950s to deal with several major civil unrest such as the Maria Hertogh riots and the Hock Lee Bus riots.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They were also deployed during Konfrontasi in the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More recently, the Gurkhas were featured widely for helping to secure the historic meeting in Singapore between US President Trump and North Korean Leader Kim in 2018.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our Gurkha officers continue to be an important part of the SPF family and I would like to pay a special tribute here for their contributions in keeping Singapore safe for more than 70 years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Before this, it was recorded in books that the untrained wives of Police constables were employed to help check women accused and were paid a dollar for conducting each search.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In the initial years, the women officers were trained to handle female offenders, record statements from victims of sexual offences and help counsel female juvenile delinquents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since their entry into the Force, our women Police officers have constantly pushed against boundaries to reach greater heights in what used to be a male-dominated profession.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to coping with the heavy workload that comes as a Police officer, many of our policewomen must cope with a second shift when they go home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite these challenges, they continue to serve and lead with distinction, and keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Incidentally, there is a Motion after this on Empowering Women.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our women Police officers have been excellent role model of breaking barriers and I ask the House to join me in thanking and honouring all our passionate women Police officers, both past and present.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is virtually impossible today to tell a VSC officer apart from a regular Police officer from the uniform he wears or the equipment he carries because they are dressed and equipped the same as their regular counterparts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unknown to many, most of our VSC officers have regular day jobs and volunteer for Police duties at night and during the weekends.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They juggle their full-time job and family commitments, on top of patrolling our streets and our territorial waters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The sacrifices of our volunteer Police officers have helped to keep Singapore’s crime rate low over the decades.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Minister Shanmugam once noted in 2017 that many law enforcement agencies around the world envy the level of faith and trust that Singaporeans have in our Police Force.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And the high levels of trust have stood the test of time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we must not take this for granted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I know how tough, difficult and exhausting the work can be.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But I have also benefited immensely from the training, the experiences and the many great friendships that I have made throughout my time in the Force, and I can see so many of them here with us today in the Gallery.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The values that SPF has ingrained in me – Courage, Loyalty, Integrity and Fairness – continue to guide me as I serve the community in a different role today.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the saying goes, once a Police officer, always a Police officer.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It has truly been an honour to have worked alongside so many dedicated Policemen and Policewomen.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As one of Singapore’s oldest institutions, it has met and overcome many great difficulties throughout its long history.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: No matter what challenges the future may bring, I know that SPF will continue to keep Singapore and all of us safe and secure for many more years to come.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza has given an excellent overview of how policing has evolved in Singapore since 1820.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is a story of growth and transformation that has enabled the Police to contribute to nation building and keep Singapore one of the safest cities in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Murali recounted acts of bravery of our officers – DSI Low, DSI Lim Siong – and paid tribute to the 125 officers who were killed in the line of duty as well as their families, and Mr Melvin Yong just highlighted the important role that many different officers played.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I rise to speak in support of this Motion and to add a personal perspective as someone who has served in the Singapore Police Force for 17 years, including five when I was on course or seconded to MOE.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Listening to Mr Patrick Tay recount how his pager sounded when he was in the cinema with his then-girlfriend reminded me of how my own dates with my girlfriend were also interrupted very often that way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But I am sure that many of our officers today will be interrupted by more than just a pager.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was telling my children about this pager story and they said, "Dad, what is a pager?" I joined SPF 15 years after our Independence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The old problems of street crimes, rioting and secret society activities had been brought under control, thanks to the excellent work of many of our veteran officers, including many of them with us here today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They were really in the rough and tumble in those early years when things were very difficult.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But back in 1980, the problem of street crimes and secret society activities were still there.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But new problems like commercial crimes were on the rise as our economy took off.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was very excited to be part of this effort to implement this new way in my second year of service.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As a fresh officer, our first assignment was to do investigation and I was posted to the Central Police Division at that time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On duty one day, I was deeply disturbed to attend to a case of a badly decomposing body.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The old lady had been dead for several days in a rental cubicle in Chinatown, but no one knew until the stench was unbearable, as she was living all alone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As part of investigations, I uncovered a sum of cash and gold jewellery that she had saved up.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I tried to trace her next-of-kin to return these valuables.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What was very sad was that several "relatives" turned up to make the claim but in order to verify this, I had to take statements from them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: None could say what they had done with her or for her.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It taught me that when members of the society are isolated and relationships were not built over time, we will run into long-term problems, and when people do not care for the people around them, the Police would have a hard time trying to maintain law and order.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And just the year before this, I spent some time in Tokyo with Mr Heng Chee How, a fellow Police officer, to study the Koban system as Dr Goh Keng Swee had decided to adopt this community policing system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When we were in our second year of service, after we finished our investigation stint, we are part of this effort to set up Neighbourhood Police Posts or NPPs all over the island, one in each constituency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: NPP officers conducted house visits, checked on the well-being of citizens, gave crime prevention advice and encouraged neighbours to form Neighbourhood Watch Group, to look out for strangers and report suspicious activities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Special efforts were made to nurture the community spirit.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the kampungs, people knew each other well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But when relocated to HDB flats, they needed time to get to know one another and to adjust to a new way of life.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It was critical to build that community spirit among neighbours, to look out for one another, to look out for criminals on the prowl.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides their own efforts, the NPP officers also worked closely with grassroots advisors and volunteers, joining them to give crime prevention advice and helping to build the community spirit.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For many officers, especially detectives, it was a huge cultural change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Police officers were traditionally seen as macho gun-toting officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The friendly Policeman, out to make friends with the public, was seen as a step backward and, in fact, the NPP system was derided by some as "No Power Police". "NPP" equals to "No Power Police".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I see many of the seniors here smiling because that was the term that we used all the time at that time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the Police Commissioner then, Goh Yong Hong, persisted.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I was later interviewed by an American professor when applying for my postgraduate studies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: His question was simple: you had low crime rates in Singapore because of harsh punishment?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I took some time to explain to him that the Singapore Police had a holistic approach in dealing with law and order.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, everyone is a potential victim of crime, so Police officers spent a great deal of effort encouraging everyone to take prevention seriously.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And the Police worked with agencies to optimise the design of public spaces, especially with the HDB, to provide protection for the most vulnerable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, it is not punishment alone, but the probability of being caught.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, it depends critically on whether you can solve a crime.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Again, after several years of the NPP system, the Police have built up enough trust and confidence for the public to come forward to do their part.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, it is how our criminal justice system is organised to ensure fairness and justice.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have due processes and a public who supports taking action.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And later on, as the system evolved, the different agencies, first within MHA, the Home Team, was one that worked closely together, Central Narcotics Bureau, the Prisons and SCDF.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, Mr Tee Tua Ba, the Commissioner whom I served under, was the Director of Prisons.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He was a Policeman seconded to become Director of Prisons and when he came back, he came back with a new perspective about how we can help to reform those criminals who can be reformed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I was glad that the professor agreed with me and told me years later when we met again that he learnt a lot about our policing approach, and not to take just a broad brush approach and come to conclusions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In many communities, unfortunately, the Police treated most members of the public or segments of them as potential criminals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This sets up an antagonistic relationship, the very exact opposite of what the Police needs to rally the 99% against the 1% or less.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We made the right choices in adopting the soft policing approach of building the community to partner one another and taking action to protect one another, so as to deal with potential criminals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And this soft approach is complemented by investing in cutting edge capabilities, whether it is in intelligence or in dealing with extreme stresses and hardened criminals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, while we can speak of policing approaches, the heart of it is in the trust and confidence of the public in the Police.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This trust and confidence rest critically on the values and attributes of our officers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the years, we have selected and developed officers with integrity and to keep out corruption.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Commissioner I first served under, Mr Goh Yong Hong, had stories of him arresting those who tried to bribe him.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Implementing community policing was a big change in culture for a policeman who grew up in the 1960s, and he gave full support to this very major change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I was serving as Commander of a Police Division, the then Commissioner Tee Tua Ba initiated an empowerment movement.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He saw that as the situation that officers had to handle were becoming more complex, and that was over 20 years ago, they could not just rely on PGO, the Police General Order.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The PGO sets out what you could or could not do.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But Mr Tee felt that every situation is different and you cannot just rely on instructions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Rather, you have to know the ambit of the law, assess each situation on the ground that you encounter, exercise discretion and take the right course of action.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This was another huge cultural change, built on the earlier changes to community policing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Personally, I have learnt much over the years and particularly enjoyed my final stint in the Police as Commander of the Jurong Police Division.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The camaraderie among officers was strong and the level of dedication was outstanding.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And the public, and Members of Parliament and grassroots leaders in the Jurong area were most supportive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Every few weeks, I had the pleasure of presenting a pewter plaque to members of the public for their acts of bravery in helping us arrest criminals, including snatch thieves and molesters.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Above all, it is critical that we continue to invest in our officers the values that underpin their work: integrity, fairness, discipline, dedication.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As crimes become more cross-border and sophisticated, our officers would need to become even more skilled.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I especially thank those who served together with me during my years in the Police.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am confident that the Singapore Police Force will continue to scale new heights and keep Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, let us, as members of the public, support our frontline officers, and as Members of this House, support legislation to strengthen the capabilities of the Police and our law enforcement agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had Sir Stamford Raffles landing in 1819 and the Police force was set up in 1820; essentially set up from the very first beginnings of modern Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr de Souza outlined SPF's journey over the years and its contributions to Singapore's development.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: SPF is now a respected force with a high standard of operational excellence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Its success has to be tested by looking at the lived experiences of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have, over the years, shared with Members, probably every year, what Singaporeans feel about their surroundings, safety and security.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will come back to this point later, but I think on no account will Singaporeans want to give that up.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is a fundamental human right: to be able to walk where you wish and where you feel, man or woman, at any time of the day or night, without fear, and to allow your child to take public transport without fear.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Singaporeans' confidence in SPF is also extremely high.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is the highest level of confidence amongst all state institutions surveyed in Singapore and also the highest globally across other police forces in the study.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What we have, this level of safety and security, and confidence in the force, did not just happen as the natural course of events.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a result of paths taken; and also paths avoided, not taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will, in the speech: first, highlight some of the factors that have made SPF successful and have helped it keep law and order in Singapore; second, pay tribute to the contributions of SPF officers; and third, outline some of SPF's plans for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are many factors which can help or impede the performance of our Police force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, the levels of governance in society, the levels of equity and inequity, inequality, many factors like that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For the purposes of this Motion, I will not speak about these larger factors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Instead, I will take a slightly narrower focus and deal with the factors that are more closely connected with Police work and the Police as an institution.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The three factors I will touch on are: first, our criminal justice system; second, the quality of leadership in SPF; and third, maintaining trust with the community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Its operations are fundamentally influenced by the criminal justice system within the framework of which the force operates.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the criminal justice system does not work, if there is no proper due process and crimes go unpunished, then it is difficult for a police force to be effective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this context, I have often referred to a speech by the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew who said this in 1962: "In a settled and established society, law appears to be a precursor of order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Good laws lead to good order, that is the form that you will learn.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the hard realities of keeping the peace between man and man, and between authority and the individual, can be more accurately described, if the phrase were inverted to 'order and law', for without order the operation of law is impossible." Members will notice that he said, "order and law", not "law and order".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have to establish order first, then laws can work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is fair to say Mr Lee sometimes took a view similar to that which Hobbes had put out, about man in society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That philosophy underpins the changes we made to the criminal justice system which we had inherited from the British.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lot of it, I would say, is primarily due to what Mr Lee himself believed, thought through and brought about, with a deep understanding of how people actually behave, how societies work and how laws actually work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The criminal justice system we inherited has a long history, evolving over many centuries in England; we adapted, changed and, in some respects, we changed quite fundamentally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This position was based on the UK Criminal Law Revision Committee's recommendation which had then not been put into practice in the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee had said that hardened criminals could greatly hamper investigations by refusing to answer any questions; so, put the onus on them to answer the questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It encouraged suspects to be forthcoming during investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members would have seen, perhaps in TV dramas, the police will tell the suspect that he or she has a right to remain silent and if the police officers did not do so, that could become, a procedural problem and the suspect may walk free on a technicality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our position: it is in the public interest that persons under investigations by the Police tell the truth when interviewed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The change has had a big impact on how suspects behave and the entire criminal process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this context, maybe I can take the opportunity of dealing with or responding to some points that Ms Lim made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think she made the following points about video-recording of interviews (VRI), translation to other languages, resource allocation, as well as helping victims and victim impact statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Steps have been taken and further the steps will be taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since today's Motion is on SPF and 200 years, and celebrating SPF, I will not go into detail on those points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is another point that, coincidentally, forms a big part of my speech too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Lim made reference to Prof Herbert Packer's work on due process and crime control.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: While it is not so clear, I think Ms Lim would probably fall on the side of the due process model.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The approach we have taken is not ideological.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is to see what is suitable, what works in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, in 1976, the steps we took would probably be described as more akin to the crime control model.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as Ms Lim was speaking, I remembered a speech by our former Chief Justice Mr Chan Sek Keong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was a lecture in 2008 – I think Justice Chan was Chief Justice at that point – at the centenary of Mr David Marshall's birth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is what he had to say and I can do no better than what perhaps the greatest jurist Singapore has seen, said about this process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, from paragraph 13 onwards: "Before I discuss some of these amendments, let me now sketch out for you the features of the criminal justice process that was in place in Singapore before 1976.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We then had an investigative and trial process regulated by the Criminal Procedure Code and the Evidence Act which basically provided the framework for a common law trial process which was highly admired, if not revered, in England at that time." I make a point to take Members through this in some detail because if you want a safe and secure Singapore, with due process for all of us, it is important to get this fundamental principle right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because there is and there will always be a tendency to move towards much more of putting hurdles and processes in the way of the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point is to strike the right balance and I would emphasise that all Members and all Ministers for Home Affairs and Law remember these fundamental principles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why I said in my speech paths taken and paths avoided.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This paper has since been regarded as one of the most important contributions to systematic thought about criminal justice.” “The basic features are those I have just described of our criminal justice process before 1976." That means, very much, due process. "Because of the presumption of innocence, priority must be given to the protection of the accused's rights in a fair manner.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police powers of arrest and investigation should be limited to prevent potential official oppression of the individual.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Law enforcement officers and the prosecution should be held accountable to rules, procedures and guidelines to ensure fairness and consistency." And he goes on; I will skip a little bit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At paragraph 15, he said: "Marshall achieved great success under this system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it was inevitable that the prosecution would sooner or later take note of the defects (from its point of view) of the existing process which had been so ably and amply demonstrated by Marshall.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must have led the Government to rethink seriously about the objectives of the criminal justice process and how to achieve those objectives.” “Let me now introduce the other model of criminal justice process that Professor Packer had identified in his paper, viz, the crime control model." And he sets out the features. "The repression of crime should be the most important function of criminal justice because order is a necessary condition for a free society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Criminal justice should concentrate on vindicating victims' rights rather than on protecting defendants' rights.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Police powers should be expanded to make it easier to investigate, arrest, search, seize and convict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Legal technicalities that handcuff the police should be eliminated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ironically, these amendments were based on the recommendations of the 1972 Eleventh Report of the UK Criminal Law Revision Committee which the UK government had rejected." For Members' reference, those who are not lawyers, the UK Criminal Law Revision Committee comprised eminent jurists and lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They looked at the system in the UK and they came up with a set of recommendations but it was not doable in the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Singapore, many of the recommendations were passed  into law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Crime control was strengthened with the use of rebuttable and irrebuttable resumptions in substantive offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These developments, together with better and more dedicated and efficient law enforcement have reduced the crime rate over the years and have made Singapore a safer place to live in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You might think that this statement is somewhat simplistic, but many people would agree that law enforcement in Singapore, although not perfect, is among the best in the world." That is the view of the Chief Justice, as he was, in 2008.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is not to say that therefore crime control becomes the be-all and end-all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, you must have fairness in the system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is a question of finding the right balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would ask Members to carefully consider what is suitable for our society when seeking to strike the right balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The right balance should not be guided by pure ideology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It should be guided by what works, what is fair, what is right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have a system today: trained judges, a defence bar, rules of process, procedure, presumption of innocence except in the context of, say, drug trials where presumption of innocence is there but the accused has got to go and prove specific factors because those are within his knowledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in corruption trials, also a reversal of onus of proof.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will be not only inaccurate, it will be hubris.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we are constantly refining, constantly trying to find the right balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the right balance also changes when society changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our philosophy is that the Police investigations should not be made into a series of technical hurdles which have to be cleared.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it must be a clear and fair process that helps to arrive at the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think all Members will agree that it is a question of balance and it is really a question of how you strike that balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have, for example, talked about, implemented, in some cases, initiatives like VRI, the Appropriate Adult Scheme, other initiatives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of these will help in the fairness in the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another example that I would put forward in going back to my point about the law enforcement framework within which the Police operate, is that tough penalties that have been introduced to deal with serious crimes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke about drugs, corruption and many other offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The penalties were changed and, where necessary, onus of proof was reversed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also have preventive detention, the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act adapted from British laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead, we have trials presided over by professional judges, who are better able to handle the complex issues for a more reliable fact-finding process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It lessens the theatrics, reduces the risk of injustice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have the institutions required for an effective judicial justice system: the judiciary, the public prosecution service, the bar associations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a result, we have a criminal justice system which has worked well for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is constant work, constant refining, constant tending and it will continue to have to be so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the system does not work well and criminals walk away because the system is corrupt or weak, then Police morale and discipline will go down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have only given a few examples of this framework but Members can assume that there have been many changes that have been very substantive that has led to the system we have today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let me now move to this context of SPF 200.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second key factor behind SPF's success is the quality of officers in SPF and the quality of its leadership.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The focus by Mr Lee and his team was on building not just the size of the Police force upon Independence but also the quality of officers and leadership in SPF.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: High quality does not only mean educational qualifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need qualities of character, a sense of purpose and you must be able to handle the pressure and perform on the job.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1972, seven years after Independence, and again I quote Mr Lee addressing Police officers at the Police Dining-in, I quote, "There are certain virtues in the force which never changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must have high morals, it must be proud of itself and it cannot be proud of itself if it has not got the right leadership.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must have that sense of purpose that comes out of men trained on a common doctrine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it must have a sense of continuity." Almost 40 years later, in 2011, that his final Police Dining-in, Mr Lee said, "We cannot have a situation where the criminals are smarter and better resourced than you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we do not recruit strong officers with the moral fibre and a sense of purpose, you will go downhill very fast." In the 40 years in between and before, these lessons were taken to heart and applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, there is rigour in who gets to become a Police officer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SPF also tries to ensure that good officers move up, regardless of their entry rank.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It implemented the unified rank structure in 2016, went beyond academic qualifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It provides faster progression through the ranks for officers who perform well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once you are in service, how you perform should matter more than your qualifications when you first came in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SPF also has a scholarship scheme – prestigious, competitive, highly sought after.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some who spoke earlier on this Motion – Members of Parliament Murali Pillai, Melvin Yong, Patrick Tay – were all scholars, and of course, the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SPF sent him on his first trip overseas to Cambridge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As a side note, if I may say so, one of the problems that SPF is finding is that other services are increasingly looking at SPF.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because apart from the Deputy Prime Minister, the Head of Civil Service and various other officers, Permanent Secretaries and those in other Ministries have come from SPF.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suppose the approach we have to take is that we spot, we groom, we invest, we train and then, we should be glad that they are taken by others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They serve in every division, including Specialist Divisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other photo is that of Sergeant Anna Anthony from the Community Policing Unit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Going back to Siti Aisyah, she is 30 years old.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Her childhood dream was to be a Police officer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She volunteered for the ERT Conversion Course which is tough and she is the first ERT Officer in Woodlands Division.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: ERT officers like her are trained in tactical and counter-assault skills.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She patrols in public places with her gear which is up to 17 kilogrammes and she maintains her IPPT Gold and Marksman qualifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She is also a Physical Training Instructor, a Police Defence Tactics Instructor and a Range Safety Officer and highly regarded among her peers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: SPF actively grooms its officers for leadership positions in the SPF.
